newsitem.title: ITALY: POLL-Next Italy discount rate cut seen in autumn.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Next Italy discount rate cut seen in autumn.

text.p: The Bank of Italy's 50 basis point cut in its official discount rate is unlikely to be the last in 1997 but markets will have to wait until towards the end of the year for the next one, analysts said.
The central bank lowered the discount rate to 6.25 percent and the fixed term advances or Lombard rate to 7.75 percent after markets closed on Friday evening, the fourth cut in just under a year.
Eleven analysts polled by Reuters on Monday said they expected the next reduction to be for 50-75 basis points, which would take the discount rate down to 5.50/5.75 percent.
Analysts said Friday's cut, being limited to 50 basis points, allowed the market to expect further reductions.

"The Bank of Italy is confirming a policy of extreme prudence, making the lowering of rates conditional on developments in public finances and exchange rate stability. For that reason I don't expect any new moves before September 30," said Martino Dolfini at Chase here.
The government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi has to present its 1998 budget to parliament by the last day of September. The package must then ratified by the end of the year.
Prodi has said the budget law will include the results of negotiations on welfare spending reforms which are currently being discussed by the government, trades unions and employers.
Alfred Granata at Banca di Roma said an autumn reduction could be for between 50 and 100 basis points depending on conditions on the international financial markets.

"The markets know there could be other cuts only if the conditions for doing so are sustained and they also know that the Bank of Italy's priority remains structural reforms in public finances," Granata said.
The lira and Btp government bonds, back from record highs registered last week, showed a limited reaction to Friday's cut in their first official trading session after the news.

Dealers said a cut had pretty much been priced into the market, leaving the BTP September future on LIFFE 10 basis points up on the day at 134.18 by 1300 GMT and the lira a fraction firmer from Friday, at 976 per mark.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio had previously cited concern that embers of inflation still existed as a reason for not easing sooner.
But analysts doubted fears that an upturn in inflation would work against the possibility of more cuts.
"In the second half of the year there will be an upturn in prices for statistical reasons but the year on year rate will still stay below two percent," Ilaria Fornari at JP Morgan said.
Inflation is currently around its lowest levels for about 30 years, after preliminary data for June showed it running at 1.4 to 1.5 percent year on year.

The central bank trimmed rates in January this year but analysts said it may have cause to hesitate in making a third cut in 1997 while it waited for a more definite framework to emerge for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

"If, as it seems, Fazio is looking above all at what's going on in Europe, the vigil for the next reduction could go on until February when we'll have more precise data to work out which countries fulfil the criteria for entering EMU," Andrea Marchetti of Credito Italiano said.
Marchetti said he doubted the central bank would make any further discount rate reductions this year.
Following are the results of the poll:
1 - Do you expect more cuts in the discount rate by the year end?
Yes 10
No 1
2 - If yes, when do you expect the next cut?
September/October 4
Towards year end 6
3 - How much do you expect the discount rate to fall by the year end?
50 basis points 4
75 bps 3
100 bps 2
125 bps 1
Participants were BancaRoma, Bank of America, Cariplo, Centrosim, Chase, BCI, Credito Italiano, JP Morgan, Nomura, San Paolo and Stone & McCarthy.
